    To remain globally competitive while adapting to a changing climate and the GLA’s draft London Plan, the Square Mile must embrace tree-lined streets, living walls, and retrofitted skyscrapers, says Greg Pitt

    London is used to change, transforming from a Roman settlement into a global financial centre.

    The GLA’s draft London Plan gives a good indication of what’s next for the capital – setting out a vision for a city that will be greener and denser by 2050.

    But what does this really mean for the Square Mile – already one of the densest areas of London, defined by sky-high towers rather than leafy parks?

    As the economic powerhouse of the UK, growth within the City should not be constrained if London is to remain globally competitive. Retaining and attracting businesses through swanky new development is important, but the draft Plan doesn’t shy away from the fact this must be balanced with the need for the Square Mile to adapt to a changing climate.

    Time for planners and architects to get creative.

    Temperatures rising

    London is bracing itself for regular 40C heatwaves by 2050, and the iconic glass skyscrapers that dominate the skyline will bear the brunt of our sweltering summers. Conventional air conditioning can act as an easy fix, but the draft London Plan makes it clear that we need to be doing more to ensure our buildings are fit for the future. 

    Part of the solution can be provided at street level. The Square Mile lacks the open land and undeveloped fringes of most London boroughs, so meeting targets for wildlife corridors and urban greening will require an integrated approach that builds nature into London’s streets and rooftops. 

    Think more tree-lined cycle lanes, pocket parks breaking up pavements and living walls on skyscrapers. Increasing green infrastructure across London, including tree canopy and planting, would create cool microclimates around buildings that offer a respite from the hot summers while improving air quality and enhancing biodiversity.  

    Stantec saw the impact of this firsthand in Denver while designing the public realm along the iconic 16th Street. The project introduced over 200 trees made up of 10 different species, supported by an innovative pavement and soil system that provided more than twenty times the amount of uncompacted soil typically available to urban trees.

    Through using public areas to make Denver’s commercial heart more resilient to climate change, one of the city’s most well-known streets has had its economic resilience strengthened too, becoming more vibrant and welcoming for all users – an ambition the Square Mile shares.

    Solutions in the sky

    To fully meet the Plan’s requirements, we also need to be looking up to the City’s skyline – allowing skyscrapers to take on the role of trees in an urban forest.

    This is a challenge faced by cities around the world, and examples from global financial and commercial hubs show you don’t have to choose between density and climate resilience. In fact, future economic strength will increasingly depend on climate resilience – proving that growth, climate adaptation and world-class commercial development can be one side of the same coin.

    Singapore’s Marina One offers an example of climate resilient office buildings, with glass surfaces broken up by green terraces and planting that reduces exposure to the sun and cools the surrounding air. Closer to home, the renovation of the former HSBC tower in Canary Wharf shows how landscaped terraces and retrofitting can enable us to develop more sustainably, with the scheme set to become one of the world’s largest low-carbon office transformations.

    A city facing new extremes

    These greener buildings don’t just help with the heat. In our famously wet country, they also have a role to play in managing rain and more inclement weather. 

    The draft London Plan sets out how new developments must contribute to reducing London’s flood risk, including by using features like green roofs and rain gardens to hold rainwater before it can gradually drain away. 

    Solutions like Denver’s pavement system and Singapore’s hanging gardens directly support this while making the cities more visually appealing too.

    By promoting this approach, the draft Plan offers a glimpse into a future where development is increasingly judged on climate resilience, as well as commercial value.

    The City’s ability to adapt is what has made it one of the most enduring financial hubs in the world.  To ensure we are adequately equipped to grasp the opportunities the next chapter presents, it must be ready to evolve again.

    California has rejected wealth taxes in referendum in a referendum where the ‘no’ campaign was largely funded by self-interested billionaires. It’s the right result for the wrong reason, says Kristian Niemietz

    The final results are not in yet, but unless the remaining uncounted votes are wildly out of the tune with the counted ones, California’s wealth tax proposal has been defeated at the ballot box. 

    ‘Proposition 40’ would have meant a one-off tax of five per cent on net wealth above a threshold of $1bn, payable by people who were residents of California in the beginning of 2026, meaning that leaving the state in order to avoid the tax would not be an option. 

    For those of us who are critical of the current wealth tax fad, though, this referendum victory could be a poisoned chalice, emboldening supporters rather than discouraging them. The opposition may win the referendum, but lose the political narrative. 

    California is home to about 260 billionaires, and the No side in the referendum relied heavily on donations from them, or more precisely, a prominent subset of them. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone contributed over $100m to the campaign. Additional donations from reasonably well-known super-rich people brought the total campaign budget up to about $300m, which enabled them to easily out-spend the pro side by a ratio of almost ten to one. 

    In one sense, the reliance on billionaire support is wholly unsurprising. Suppose you think wealth taxes are a bad idea, and you want to run a campaign against them. Who do you ask for financial support? Of course that’s going to be the people who have both the money to support your campaign, and an obvious interest in doing so. The average Joe is not going to spend money on preventing the introduction of a tax that they will never pay. Sure, opponents will argue that the economic cost of a wealth tax will ultimately fall on the average Joe, not just – or even primarily – on the billionaires who make the transfer to the tax office. But that argument will not be remotely obvious to most people: it takes a lot of explaining, and in order to explain it, you need to be able to finance a campaign first. You are not running a year-long education campaign about tax incidence, second-order effects and unintended consequences. 

    However, while convenient in the short term, opposing wealth taxes in this way comes at a long-term cost. By relying so heavily on the support of people who have an obvious financial self-interest in opposing wealth taxes, you contribute to the impression that financial self-interest is the only reason why someone could possibly oppose wealth taxes. In that way, you play into the hands of their most populist proponents. 

    Slopulism

    I have debated wealth taxes multiple times over the past 18 months or so, on TV, on the radio, at university debating societies. I have found that different people support wealth taxes for very different reasons, and in different ways. The more fair-minded supporters will accept that there are serious, legitimate economic arguments against them. It is just that they – and this is where we differ – do not see this as a reason for abandoning the idea altogether. For them, it is just a reason to be ultra-careful in the design of a wealth tax, and to get the details right. 

    Polanski-style slopulists, on the other hand, refuse to debate in such terms. They will tell a story in which modern politics is a battle between The People, who are good and pure, and The Billionaires, who are rapacious, extractive and divisive. The Billionaires impoverish The People, and then they engage in a divide-and-rule strategy, using their obscene wealth to distort public debate, and foment Hate And Division among The People. In that version of events, economic arguments are just disguised class interests. If you oppose wealth taxes, you must be either a plutocrat defending your ill-gotten gains, or you must be a mercenary in their pay. 

    If I tried to peddle a story along those lines, I would treat the California referendum as a godsend. Had Proposition 40 won, its supporters would now have to deal with the practicalities of a wealth tax, and in due course, with a backlash from disappointed campaigners. Now, the Polanskiites will interpret the result as just another example of billionaires subverting democracy. They will interpret the very defeat of the wealth tax as an illustration of why a wealth tax is necessary in the first place. 

    That’s why, as a critic of wealth taxes, I have to admit that I almost wish the other side had won. 

    Dr Kristian Niemietz is the outgoing editorial director of the Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA). He is the author of the report ‘Fool’s Gold: The case against the wealth tax, and suggestions for alternatives’.

    Betfred have pulled out of sponsoring the Derby, citing Chancellor John Healey’s tax hikes at last month’s Budget.

    The gambling firm signed a deal, in two parts, to sponsor five major racing meets in the United Kingdom known as the British Classics. Feature races include the Derby and Oaks at Epsom, the St Leger – which this year celebrated its 250th year this summer – at Doncaster and both the 1,000 and 2,000 Guineas at Newmarket.

    But tax hikes issued by both Rachel Reeves and Healey at consecutive Budgets have squeezed available spend on horse racing, resulting in Betfred – who are owned by the UK’s top taxpayer Fred Done – pulling their sponsorship. 

    A Betfred spokesman said: “Following successive tax rises for the betting industry, and in particular the increase to machine games duty at the most recent budget, it is with great sadness that we have taken the difficult decision not to proceed with a three-year renewal of our sponsorship of the British Classics.

    “It is not a decision we wanted to make, but the cumulative cost of government policy has left us with no choice.”

    Betfred ditch racing

    Healey announced a five per cent increase to machine games duty at the Budget last month, meaning a hike of 25 per cent will be implemented once Reeves’ previous 20 per cent raid is taken into account.

    And it comes after Betfred pulled out of sponsoring rugby’s Super League, which has cost the code £1m per year.

    Done told the Financial Times: “Do you think when there’s no betting shops punters will stop betting? The answer is no. They will find a way to bet, like in the prohibition,”

    “There won’t be the controls [when those gamblers go to the black market], there won’t be the taxes and there won’t be funding for [horse] racing.”

    Amy Starkey of the Jockey Club said: “While we are naturally disappointed that Betfred have taken the decision not to renew their sponsorship of the Derby and the Guineas Festival at Newmarket, we understand their reasons for doing so and know this was not an easy decision for them.”

    “We are currently in conversations with a number of interested prospective partners that share our ambitions for the future of both events.”

    Chery’s new electric SUV is comfortable, roomy and loaded with kit, and it’s a close relative of the Jaecoo 7 that topped Britain’s sales chart in September.     Chery’s new electric SUV is comfortable, roomy and loaded with kit, and it’s a close relative of the Jaecoo 7 that topped Britain’s sales chart in September. I drove a pre-production car in China, and if you want an EV with a name people will ask about in the company car park, it deserves a look, though the price will decide whether it deserves your money.

    Lepas L6 EV price and UK launch date

    The Lepas L6 EV is a comfortable, roomy electric family SUV with a long kit list and an official range of up to 279 miles, and on my drive it earned a place on any electric SUV shortlist. The steering is its weak spot, and the value case can’t be judged until Lepas names a price.

    That price hasn’t been announced yet, but order books are due to open in the final quarter of this year, and dealers are already taking registrations of interest. The brand is on sale here already with the L8, a bigger plug-in hybrid SUV that costs £34,900 in Essence trim and £37,900 as an Elevate, which shows where Lepas is pitching itself. Motorpoint expects the L6 to start at around £30,000 to £32,000.

    I drove a pre-production L6 EV over several days between Shanghai and Chery’s headquarters in Wuhu. It impressed me with its comfort and straightforward performance, although the steering felt artificial.

    The L6 shares its technology with the Jaecoo 7, Chery’s plug-in hybrid SUV that was the UK’s best-selling car in September, and it joins Chery, Omoda, Jaecoo and the L8 in the company’s push into Britain. Its electric rivals include the Skoda Elroq, Kia EV3 and Volkswagen ID.4.

    Who makes Lepas, and why does it exist?

    Lepas is Chery’s newest brand, launched in April 2025. At the 2026 Chery International User Summit in Wuhu, which was the other reason I was in China, I asked Zhong Wei, Lepas’s deputy chief executive, why the world needed it.

    For Mr Zhong, the brand reflects a shift in what buyers want. As people become more discerning, he says, they look for a car that expresses their personality and taste as well as getting them from A to B. Chery’s existing brands can’t satisfy every customer in the same way, he explained, so the company created a marque with its own identity, built around what he calls an elegant lifestyle of new-energy vehicles, intelligent technology and a more considered ownership experience.

    That’s a big ask in Britain, where plenty of company-car drivers and private buyers have stuck with European badges for years. They’ll want to know what a Lepas is worth after three years, and because the brand is so new here, there’s no track record to tell them.

    What is the Lepas L6 EV like to drive?

    I drove the L6 EV on multi-lane expressways, across the flat roads of the Yangtze River Delta and along more scenic mountain routes.

    It felt comfortable throughout, and acceleration was strong enough to make overtaking straightforward without the abrupt surge some electric cars produce. It also stayed composed on faster roads, in rain or shine (the part of China we were in seemed to deliver four seasons in one day). The cabin had enough room for four of us and our luggage, so it made a relaxed family car.

    The L6’s main weakness is its steering, which lacks the feedback you get from some European brands. If all you want is a comfortable, easy SUV, you’ll barely notice, but if you enjoy a more connected drive, it’s the part of the L6 most likely to disappoint.

    These impressions are based on a pre-production car, so the finished UK version may have different suspension and steering settings.

    Lepas L6 EV range and charging

    The L6 pairs a 65kWh battery with an electric motor producing 217PS and 275Nm of torque. Lepas quotes a 0 to 62mph time of 7.9 seconds and an official WLTP range of up to 279 miles.

    Driving in China isn’t always easy, especially in downpours (it’s almost as tricky as London), so I kept my eyes on the road rather than the instruments for much of the trip. We covered 360km (223 miles) in a day on fairly fast expressways, in humid weather with the air-con running the whole time, and the range never became a worry.

    Efficiency on that route hovered around 3.5 miles per kWh. That works out at roughly 225 miles from a full battery, about 50 miles short of the official figure, which is a fair result for fast driving in the heat with the air-con on, and it should cover most commutes for several days between charges.

    Maximum DC charging power is 120kW, and Lepas says a 30 to 80 per cent top-up takes about 22 minutes. How the L6 copes with a British winter and UK chargers is something I’ll find out on the UK-spec drive.

    Lepas L6 EV interior, boot space and technology

    The dashboard has a 13.2-inch touchscreen and an 8.88-inch digital driver’s display, and the system is quick and easy to use. There’s also a Hello Lepas voice assistant, which I didn’t try because I don’t speak Chinese. The cameras are crystal clear, making parking a doddle even when you’re jetlagged in the middle of a Chinese service station, and I think they’d earn their keep in tight city streets and underground car parks, especially in London.

    There are only two trims, Essence and Elevate. Both get 19-inch alloy wheels, a panoramic sunroof, a heated steering wheel and windscreen, 50W wireless phone charging, a 540-degree camera system, 22 driver-assistance functions and a 3.3kW vehicle-to-load socket. The Elevate adds heated and ventilated, electrically adjustable front seats, leather-effect upholstery, a power tailgate, an eight-speaker Sony stereo and parking assistance that includes remote parking. My pre-production car seemed to mix equipment from both, with fabric seats in place of the Elevate’s leather-effect finish.

    We drove four-up for most of the trip, and there’s room for three across the back seat. All our luggage went into the 410-litre boot, which grows to 1,334 litres with the rear seats folded (we didn’t need to try that), and a 99-litre compartment under the floor is handy for charging cables or a work laptop you’d rather keep out of sight.

    Lepas L6 EV company car tax and running costs

    For company-car drivers, the L6 sits on the same 4 per cent benefit-in-kind rate as any electric car in the 2026/27 tax year, rising to 5 per cent from April 2027. If it were priced at £35,000, in line with the L8, that would be roughly £560 a year in tax for a 40 per cent taxpayer and £280 for a basic-rate one.

    Private buyers will want to see the price before judging value, but the warranty is reassuring, with seven years or 100,000 miles on the car and eight years or 100,000 miles on the battery. RAC roadside cover comes free for the first year and can be renewed for up to seven years if you service the car at a Lepas dealer.

    Is the Lepas L6 EV worth buying?

    The L6 EV has the makings of a credible electric family SUV, with useful performance, a practical cabin and a long list of standard kit. The big unanswered question is value.

    What we like

    • A claimed range of up to 279 miles, and about 225 miles in hot, fast real-world driving.
    • Comfortable cruising and plenty of room for a family and its luggage.
    • A long list of standard technology, including a 540-degree camera system that makes parking easy.

    What worries us

    • Steering that felt artificial.
    • No confirmed UK price.
    • Unknown resale values for a brand that’s new to Britain.

    If the L6 is on your list for when orders open, find out what your current car is worth with Regit’s free valuation, so you know how much a part-exchange could knock off the price.

    Verdict

    The Lepas L6 EV deserves a place on your electric SUV shortlist, because it’s comfortable and spacious, has a boot you wouldn’t turn your nose up at, and comes with a camera system that takes the stress out of tight streets and underground car parks. The steering needs work, though, and the L6 still has to prove itself on British roads.

    Until Lepas confirms UK pricing, the value case is a blank, and with the L8 already at £34,900 the L6 needs to come in well below that. Get the number right and it could be a serious alternative to better-known electric SUVs such as the Skoda Elroq. I’ll be driving a UK-spec car in the coming weeks, and I’ll update this review when I have.

    Whoever bought a BMW i7 new three years ago has watched well over half its price disappear, which is rotten luck for them and a gift for anyone shopping second-hand. Better still, a luxury EV registered before April 2025 escapes a tax that a new one pays for five years.

    If you’ve ever fancied a BMW i7, the used market has made it a lot more realistic. Three-year-old cars are listed at dealers from about £45,000, according to AutoUncle listings we checked on 5 November, while the cheapest new i7 costs £104,230. Figures Auto Express published on 29 October show it’s part of a pattern, because the i7, Porsche Taycan, BMW i5, Audi e-tron GT and Mercedes EQS and EQE are all expected to be worth less than a third of their price new after three years and 36,000 miles.

    Those Auto Express numbers are forecasts of what a car bought new today will fetch in part-exchange, set against its average list price, or the price of one version where it names one. Dealers ask more than part-exchange value, and plenty of these cars were sold with hefty discounts, so not every first owner has lost quite this much, but the size of the drop shows you where the bargains are.

    Which luxury EVs lose the most value

    1. Porsche Taycan

    Average price new £162,255, expected value after three years about £50,475, so it’s expected to lose about £111,780.

    No electric car in Auto Express’s figures loses more cash, though the average is dragged up by Turbo S and Turbo GT versions costing well over £150,000, and 2023 cars are listed from about £51,000. A 2023 car is the version before the 2024 update, which Porsche says brought up to 35% more range, so look up the official range for the exact car you’re looking at rather than going by a new one’s brochure.

    2. BMW i7

    Average price new £143,530, expected value after three years about £46,050, so it’s expected to lose about £97,480.

    AutoUncle showed 21 three-year-old i7s for sale on 5 November, from £43,998, with most between about £47,000 and £63,000. Auto Express reckons the i7 is the wiser used buy of the two big electric limousines, ahead of the Mercedes EQS. Our motoring reporter Tim Barnes-Clay reviewed the facelifted 2026 i7, and two of the changes he found matter if you’re buying an older one. The update lifted BMW’s range figure to as much as 452 miles from 388, so a 2023 car won’t go as far on a charge, but it also took away the iDrive rotary controller, which Tim missed and which a 2023 car still has.

    3. BMW i5

    Average price new £110,045, expected value after three years about £34,650, so it’s expected to lose about £75,395.

    The i5 is the electric 5 Series, long the default choice in the executive car park. Auto Express’s average is higher than the list price of even the top i5 M60 Touring (£98,425), so treat the cash figure as rough, but keeping about 31% of its value is the number that matters. It only went on sale in late 2023, so used ones are mostly 2024 cars or newer, and that’s fine for tax, because what counts is the date the car was first registered.

    4. Audi e-tron GT

    Price new £107,875 for the S e-tron GT, expected value after three years about £33,150, so it’s expected to lose about £74,725.

    The e-tron GT shares its underpinnings with the Taycan, so it’s the closest thing to a Porsche with four rings on the bonnet. Auto Express’s figures are for today’s S e-tron GT, while 2023 cars are the earlier e-tron GT quattro, and used ones are thinner on the ground. One we found, a December 2023 car with about 13,700 miles, was up for £46,850, which AutoUncle reckons is about £5,000 more than it’s worth.

    5. Mercedes EQS

    Price new £104,540 for the EQS 450+ Premium, expected value after three years about £32,375, so it’s expected to lose about £72,165.

    The EQS gives you S-Class space and quiet without an engine, and 2023 EQS 450+ saloons were listed from about £41,500 on 5 November. Auto Express isn’t a fan, though, and says rivals including the i7 are simply better all-round packages.

    6. Mercedes EQE

    Price new £86,615 for the EQE 350+ AMG Line Night Edition, expected value after three years about £26,850, so it’s expected to lose about £59,765.

    The EQE is the smaller EQS, roughly an electric E-Class, and it’s the cheapest way into this club. AutoUncle had 29 three-year-old EQE 300s for sale on 5 November, between about £29,000 and £37,000, which is about what a new Volkswagen Golf costs. Cheaper electric cars lose even more in percentage terms, led by the Lexus UX 300e, and we’ve rounded those up separately.

    Why a used luxury EV is cheaper to tax

    What matters is the date on the log book. GOV.UK’s vehicle tax rate tables say any electric car first registered before 1 April 2025 never pays the £440 Expensive Car Supplement, however much it cost new, so it pays the £200 standard rate. Electric cars registered since then pay £10 in their first year, then £640 a year for the next five if their list price was over £50,000, which covers every car on this list.

    That’s £2,200 over five years that a car registered before April 2025 never pays. October’s Budget raises the standard rate to £210 from April 2027, but the gap stays, and our guide to this year’s car tax changes covers the rest of the rates. Check the first registration date on the V5C before you buy, because an i5 registered in March 2025 and one registered in April look the same on the forecourt but don’t cost the same to tax.

    In London, any electric car is ULEZ-free, and the Congestion Charge is £13.50 a day rather than £18 as long as the car is registered for Auto Pay, while plug-in hybrids pay the full £18. That matters if you want a 7 Series, because in 2023 BMW UK sold it only as the electric i7 or as a plug-in hybrid such as the 750e. Drive a 2023 750e into the zone on about 230 working days a year and the charge comes to £4,140, against £3,105 in an i7, so the i7 saves £1,035. Add the £440 supplement the 750e pays until its sixth year on the road and the i7 comes out almost £1,500 a year ahead. From April 2028, though, electric cars will also pay 3p a mile on top of road tax, which is about £270 a year if you cover 9,000 miles, and Regit has worked out what pay-per-mile tax will cost you at other mileages.

    What to check before you buy

    A 2023 car will only just have had its first MOT, so the service history tells you more than the MOT record. Ask for a battery health report, which shows how much of the original capacity is left, and check how long the battery warranty has to run. Make sure both charging cables come with the car, look at the tyres (heavy EVs get through them quickly) and get an insurance quote before you fall for one, because a car that’s cheap to buy is still expensive to insure.

    When you’ve found the one, put its number plate into Regit’s free car valuation and you’ll know whether the dealer’s price for that i7 or EQS is fair before you start haggling.

    Our verdict

    Let someone else pay for the first three years. A 2023 BMW i7 from about £45,000 is our pick, because it has a back seat built for being driven around in, keeps the rotary controller the new one has lost and costs £200 a year to tax. If you’d rather drive than be driven, the Taycan from about £51,000 is the more exciting car, and the EQE from £29,000 is the cheapest way in, but whichever you choose, get the battery checked and the insurance quoted before you sign.

    Mortgage holders are bracing for a “painful rise” in payments after the Bank of England tightened monetary policy for the first time since mid-2023.

    The Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee raised interest rates to four per cent in a bid to stop inflation spiralling out of control amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. 

    But the decision will cause a further squeeze on home owners, who are already struggling against rising bills, as higher borrowing drives up mortgage costs.

    Around 2.3m households are due to come off fixed rate deals by the end of 2027, and could face higher bills when it comes to remortgaging. 

    The majority of borrowers secured deals during periods of low rates, meaning they could see monthly repayments rise by hundreds of pounds.

    Polling from City AM/ Freshwater Strategy, found 29 per cent of people believed they would be unable to afford the rise in bills off the back of the rise in mortgage bills.

    According to Moneyfacts, the average two-year fixed mortgage rate stood at 5.87 per cent at the beginning of November. The average five-year fix was at six per cent.

    Fixed mortgage rates are largely influenced by financial markets’ expectations of future interest rates and don’t reflect immediate shifts in the base rate. But the hawkish split of Monetary Policy Committee members, who all voted for a hike, may push fixed rates up as lenders price in the prospect of a higher rate regime.

    “For mortgage holders, today’s decision will add to the pressure on household finances, particularly…those approaching the end of a fixed rate deal,” said Alexandra Loydon, group advice director at St James’s Place.

    “With household budgets already stretched, even a small increase in monthly repayments could add to financial pressures.”

    Tracker mortgage woes

    The small number of households that are on tracker mortgages can expect a near-immediate rise in repayments. The products follow the fluctuation of the Bank’s central rate.

    Tracker mortgage holders can expect a £30.72 monthly increase to their mortgage repayments, according to UK Finance.

    Financial advisers said that while the sharp rise can be painful in the short term, those willing to hold on until rates come down again could secure a better deal in the long run.

    Samuel Mather Holgate, managing director of advice firm Mather & Murray Financial, said: “For borrowers who can tolerate some uncertainty, a tracker mortgage could prove considerably better value, particularly if inflation pressures ease.”

    But, David Hollingworth, associate director of L&C Mortgages, said there is “no guarantee that rates don’t keep on climbing”, warning people to only take on a tracker mortgage if they can handle the financial uncertainty.

    Variable deals

    Meanwhile, those on a standard variable rate (SVR), where the rate is set at the discretion of the lender, could also face higher repayments.

    John Fraser-Tucker, head of mortgages at Mojo Mortgages, warned that letting your mortgage roll onto a SVR could “easily be the most expensive mistake a borrower could make right now”.

    Roughly, 470,000 deals are on SVR, and if a lender decides to pass on the 0.25 percentage point increase in full, the average homeowner will see their monthly repayments increase by £14.28.

    “The rate rise is likely to mean people with variable rate mortgages see another painful rise in their outgoings, so will need to find savings elsewhere,” said Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at AJ Bell.

    “This is easier said than done, because prices have already been climbing, particularly at the pumps, and life is set to get harder in January, when a horrible hike in energy prices turns the screw on people’s budgets.”

Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:13:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Researchers tracked the passwords 154 people used online for an average of 147 days and found them logging into 26 websites with fewer than 10 unique passwords — roughly 60 percent were reused outright or built from pieces of passwords they were already using elsewhere https://siliconcanals.com/d-researchers-tracked-the-passwords-154-people-used-online-for-an-average-of-147-days-and-found-them-logging-into-26-websites-with-fewer-than-10-unique-passwords-roughly-60-percent-were-reused/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:40 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109740

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That January 2022 round is the most recent outside capital the company has raised at scale; the 2025 results suggest it hasn’t needed another one since.

The first profit, and how thin it was

That changed with the 2025 financial year. According to Bolt’s own results, reported in coverage from Trade with Estonia, the company took €2.27 billion in revenue across more than 50 countries, a 14 percent increase on the year before, and posted its first-ever annual net profit: €920,000. Set against €2.27 billion in revenue, that works out to a margin of roughly four hundredths of one percent, the kind of number that is technically profitable and not much more. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. Villig described the underlying business as having reached a $14 billion gross merchandise value run-rate with two consecutive years of positive cash flow, arguably the more meaningful signal for a company at Bolt’s stage than the net income line itself.

What a four-hundredths-of-a-percent margin actually means

A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. The accounts do not reveal whether Bolt targeted that result or whether it could sustain growth without further external financing. They show a small net profit and positive operating cash flow for the year, not permanent financial independence. It hasn’t settled every question that scale raises, either.

In November 2024, a UK employment tribunal ruled that Bolt’s drivers qualify as workers rather than independent contractors — a ruling on status only, with compensation still to be set at a separate hearing. Leigh Day, the law firm representing roughly 15,000 drivers in the claim, estimates the compensation owed could exceed £200 million, or upwards of £15,000 per driver on average, according to Leigh Day’s own statement. Whether a margin this thin holds, thickens, or gets eaten by exactly that kind of regulatory ruling as Bolt pushes into new cities, verticals and eventually autonomous vehicles is the open question its 2025 results don’t settle either way.

]]> A country of fewer than 1.4 million people has produced ten billion-dollar startups — about 7 for every million residents, more than three times the US rate — and the first of them was a voice-call app a handful of engineers built in Tallinn in 2003. https://siliconcanals.com/n-a-country-of-fewer-than-1-4-million-people-has-produced-ten-billion-dollar-startups-about-7-for-every-million-residents-more-than-three-times-the-us-rate/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 10:00:24 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109711

Estonia ranks second in the cited per-capita tally—and first in the EU—with about 7.1 startups that have reached a billion-dollar valuation per million residents.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: The original excerpt called Estonia the world leader, although the cited per-capita tally places it second behind Liechtenstein. The article also misstated the Tiger Leap school-internet rollout; first-party history says all schools were connected by 2001.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The one that started it

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Its founders, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, co-founded the company with three Estonian engineers, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn, who built the software behind what was then an unusually good way to make free voice calls over the internet. eBay bought the company two years later for a reported $2.6 billion in upfront cash and stock (total consideration including later earn-outs was reported as high as $4.1 billion).

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

Why the count kept growing

The clearest example of that inheritance is Wise. Its co-founder Taavet Hinrikus was Skype’s first employee; his eventual co-founder, Kristo Käärmann, worked at Deloitte in London. Both were Estonians living abroad with an ordinary, irritating problem: Hinrikus was paid in euros but lived in the UK, and Käärmann was paid in pounds but had a mortgage back in Estonia in euros. According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

A pipeline that keeps producing, even without unicorns

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. Estonian startups collectively reported €3.9 billion in revenue in 2024, up 14.7 percent on the year before, according to Invest in Estonia’s own sector figures, and the sector now employs about 14,400 people directly, or roughly one in every 38 working Estonians, at an average monthly salary of €3,650, more than double the national average. Venture capital raised by Estonian startups actually fell 23 percent in 2024, to €326.6 million across 57 rounds, the lowest total in five years, a reminder that a dense unicorn count doesn’t insulate a small ecosystem from a broader European slowdown in early-stage funding. What has held up is the type of company being funded: deep technology, rather than consumer apps or fintech, took 63 percent of all startup investment in 2024, led by rounds for the delivery-robot company Starship Technologies and the green-hydrogen firm Stargate Hydrogen.

What the density figure doesn’t tell you

A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

In 2025 that website moved €10.8 billion of second-hand goods, took €1.1 billion in revenue and gave users access to more than 500,000 pick-up and drop-off points through delivery partners across Europe https://siliconcanals.com/n-in-2008-a-woman-in-vilnius-was-moving-flat-with-more-clothes-than-would-fit-so-a-friend-built-her-a-website-to-give-them-away-to-friends-in-2025-that-website-moved-e10-8-billion-of-second-hand-goods/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 07:29:09 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109710

A Lithuanian clothing-swap site born from one woman’s move became a major European secondhand marketplace, moving billions in goods and building a large delivery-partner network.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: The original headline said Vinted runs more than 500,000 parcel points; those locations belong to its delivery-partner network. The article also conflated the buyer-protection fee with the separate shipping charge.

Milda Mitkutė was changing apartments in Vilnius in 2008 and had more clothes than the new place could hold. Rather than throw them out, she wanted a way to pass them on to people she knew. A friend, the software developer Justas Janauskas, built her a website for it. “We chatted about creating a website where people could trade their pre-loved fashion with each other,” Janauskas later told Tech.eu in 2015, recalling that he was doubtful the idea would go anywhere until he asked around and found most of his friends thought it was a good one.

The two of them built the earliest version as a side project, under a Lithuanian name that translated roughly to “my clothes,” with no marketing budget and no plan beyond friends trading with friends. What tipped it into something larger was almost accidental. A couch-surfing guest from Munich learned about the site, liked it, and helped carry the idea into Germany, where it launched under its own local name, Kleiderkreisel. Other country-specific spin-offs followed the same pattern for a few years, each with its own name and its own small user base, before the company folded them together under a single brand, Vinted, as the parent business decided a fragmented set of local sites made less sense than one platform users could recognise anywhere in Europe. Vilnius stayed its home throughout.

How a free listing site turns a profit

The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. Vinted makes its money almost entirely from the buyer’s side of the transaction: a fixed fee of roughly $0.70 plus a variable fee of about 5 percent of the item’s price, charged in the buyer’s local currency (figures as of late 2025) — according to Vinted’s own Buyer Protection fee page. That fee funds Vinted’s Buyer Protection service, including secure payment handling and dispute support. Shipping is a separate charge paid by the buyer at checkout, even though the seller receives a prepaid label. It is close to the inverse of how rivals like Poshmark and Depop have historically operated, charging the seller a cut instead. Vinted also sells optional promotion to sellers who want more visibility: a feature called Closet Spotlight puts five of a seller’s listings into other users’ feeds for a week for a flat fee, and a per-item “bump” pushes a single listing up in search results, priced dynamically by category and demand.

From a hobby site to a logistics network

Underneath the fee structure sits a harder problem: getting a stranger’s old jumper from a seller’s flat to a buyer’s front door, cheaply and reliably, across dozens of countries. That has turned Vinted into as much a logistics company as a marketplace. According to the company’s own 2025 financial results, its delivery partner network now gives users access to more than 500,000 pick-up and drop-off points across Europe, and the company runs its own parcel carrier, Vinted Go, directly in five markets: Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain. In 2025 it also opened operations in Latvia, Estonia and Slovenia, seventeen years after that first Vilnius website, extending its reach into corners of Europe the original Kleiderkreisel-era patchwork of local sites never touched.

From a free site to a billion-dollar company

The money that built out Vinted’s logistics network came in stages, and the pace of it tracks how quickly investors decided the model was working. In November 2019, the company raised €128 million in a round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, with Accel, Insight Partners, Sprints Capital and Burda Principal Investments also participating, pushing its valuation past $1 billion for the first time and making it, according to the reporting on the round, Lithuania’s first unicorn. Lightspeed partner Brad Twohig said at the time the firm looked for “outlier management teams building generational companies,” a fairly standard line for a venture press release, but one that in this case was describing two people who had started out solving a problem for their own friends.

Two years later, in 2021, a further round led by EQT Growth brought in $303 million and roughly quadrupled the valuation again, to $4.5 billion, with the same core group of earlier investors returning. That was the last outside funding round before the company turned its first profit in 2023, at which point continued growth could increasingly be funded from the business itself rather than from new investors.

What the 2025 numbers actually show

Vinted’s first profitable year, by its own account, was 2023, when it reported revenue of €596.3 million and a net profit of €17.8 million, a milestone The Next Web covered as the company’s first since founding. Two years later, the picture is bigger but less straightforwardly better. Vinted moved €10.8 billion in gross merchandise value in 2025, up 47 percent on the year before, and took €1.1 billion of that as revenue, up 38 percent, almost double the 2023 figure. But net profit, which had grown substantially in the years after 2023, fell 19 percent in 2025 to €62 million, and adjusted EBITDA slipped 5 percent to €151 million. CEO Thomas Plantenga framed the trade-off plainly in the release: the company is spending on expansion, including a push into Germany, category diversification beyond clothing, and the launch of a payments wallet called Vinted Pay, rather than banking the growth as profit this year.

That is a company reinvesting in expansion while remaining profitable, not a company in trouble. It is worth naming the distinction because the two can look similar on a spreadsheet, and a 19 percent drop in profit reads very differently once it’s clear the company was profitable at all only two years earlier, and is still profitable now, just less so by design.

A platform built on other people’s closets

What the €10.8 billion figure represents is how far secondhand clothing has moved from a hobby into ordinary consumer behaviour across Europe. The company has said it intends to bring the same model to the United States next, according to Dealroom’s coverage of the 2025 results. Whether Vinted’s European logistics playbook, built over seventeen years and hundreds of thousands of parcel points, transfers to a market with a completely different postal and returns infrastructure is the open question the 2025 numbers don’t answer.

Rapidly changing feed content may increase task switching and decision-making, which can make scrolling feel mentally tiring.]]>

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.
